Family

Tantrums: what to do when a child explodes

Tantrums are normal between one and four years old. Staying calm and not giving in to screaming helps most.

The child throws themselves on the supermarket floor, screams, kicks and nothing will calm them. Few situations test parents' patience as much, especially with people watching.

Why they happen

Tantrums are very common between one and four years old. At that age, children want more and more things and have more initiative, but they cannot yet put their feelings into words or control frustration. The parts of the brain that regulate emotions take years to mature. Tiredness, hunger or changes in routine make them more likely. Most last a few minutes.

Prevention is easier

Many tantrums are predictable: they appear when a child is hungry, sleepy or tired, at transitions such as leaving the park or switching off the TV, and in places full of temptations. Giving advance warning ("five more minutes and we're going"), offering limited choices ("shoes first or coat first?") and keeping regular meal and sleep times greatly reduce how often they happen.

Parenting programmes

When tantrums are very frequent or intense, parent training programmes have good evidence. Programmes such as Triple P or The Incredible Years teach parents to reinforce positive behaviour with attention and specific praise, to set limits calmly and consistently and to use brief consequences. Several meta-analyses show they reduce children's behaviour problems and parental stress.

When to seek advice

It is worth talking to the paediatrician if tantrums remain very frequent after age five, if the child hurts themselves or others, if they last much longer than usual or if they come with language delay or other developmental difficulties.

What usually helps

  • Stay calm. Shouting or punishing mid-outburst usually prolongs it. A calm adult helps the child recover.
  • Do not give in to what triggered the tantrum. If screaming works, the child learns it is a good strategy.
  • Ensure safety and, if needed, take them somewhere quiet.
  • Name the emotion once it has passed: "you were really angry because you wanted the biscuit".
  • Prevent: give warning of changes, offer simple choices ("do you want the blue pyjamas or the red ones?") and look after sleep.
It is worth seeing the paediatrician if tantrums are very frequent after age four or five, last a long time, if the child hurts themselves or others, or if they come with language or developmental problems.

References

  1. Daniels, E., Mandleco, B. y Luthy, K. E. (2012). Assessment, management, and prevention of childhood temper tantrums. Journal of the American Academy of Nurse Practitioners, 24(10), 569–573.
  2. Asociación Española de Pediatría de Atención Primaria. Familia y Salud: Rabietas.
  3. Sanders, M. R., Kirby, J. N., Tellegen, C. L. y Day, J. J. (2014). The Triple P–Positive Parenting Program: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review, 34(4), 337–357.
  4. Belden, A. C., Thomson, N. R. y Luby, J. L. (2008). Temper tantrums in healthy versus depressed and disruptive preschoolers. Journal of Pediatrics, 152(1), 117–122.
